instrument.title: EU AI Act enforcement
instrument.thesis: What is actually enforced versus what was announced. Tracking how far Europe has stood up the law it wrote, and what has happened to anyone who broke it.
instrument.refresh_note: Updated weekly · last refresh 28 Jul 2026, 09:00 CET

what_changed: The delay is law. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 was published in the Official Journal on 24 July and entered into force on 27 July, six days before the deadline it was racing. Article 50 transparency was not moved and applies from 2 August, alongside the Commission's first power to fine a general-purpose model provider. Fines issued stayed at zero.

forward_call.this_week_expects: No fine under the Act anywhere in the EU in the first month the Commission can issue one against a general-purpose model provider, so none by 2 September.
forward_call.prior_call: The Omnibus to be published in the Official Journal before 2 August, making the delay binding.

body: The delay is law. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 was published in the Official Journal on 24 July and entered into force on 27 July, six days before the deadline it was racing. The high-risk obligations for stand-alone Annex III systems now apply from 2 December 2027, and for AI built into regulated products from 2 August 2028. Both have been postponed before a single one took effect. The call this instrument made a fortnight ago, that the text would reach the Journal in time, holds.

What that leaves is a narrower August than most readers expect, not an empty one. Article 50 was not moved. From 2 August anyone deploying a system that talks to a person, or that generates synthetic image, audio or video, owes disclosure; only the machine-readable marking of content from systems already on the market gets until 2 December. On the same day Article 101 switches on, and for the first time the Commission can fine the provider of a general-purpose model up to fifteen million euro or three percent of worldwide turnover. The power arrives exactly one year after the rules it enforces.

The enforcers, meanwhile, have caught up somewhat. Nine member states have now designated both a market surveillance and a notifying authority, against three when this instrument last counted, and Italy, Malta, Slovenia, Hungary, Lithuania and Cyprus account for most of that movement. Six still have not named anyone, a year past the deadline to do so. Prohibited practices reach 546 days in force on 2 August with no fine issued anywhere. So the question this month is no longer what the law says. It is whether a Commission that has just been handed a fining power uses it, and the position here is that it will not, not this side of September.

methodology.note: Designation status is yellow3's reading of the European Commission's consolidated list of notified authorities, cross-checked against the IAPP regulatory directory and the Future of Life Institute implementation timeline, as of the stated date. In-force dates reflect the AI Act as amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 and in force since 27 July 2026. This tracks legal status and public enforcement actions, not compliance behaviour inside companies. A fine is counted only when a competent authority or the Commission has publicly confirmed it.
methodology.source_line: Sources: Official Journal, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744; European Commission AI Act Service Desk; artificialintelligenceact.eu (Future of Life Institute). As of 28 Jul 2026
